title: Before You Start
description: Never touched a terminal? Start here: typing commands, reading them, and peeking at config files. No coding required.

lessons.title: What's a terminal?
lessons.description: Type commands instead of clicking, and find your way around folders.

theory.title: A window you talk to with text
theory.body:
Hi, I'm **Kip**, a hermit crab whose shell is a terminal. A **terminal** is a text window where you **type commands** instead of clicking buttons.

When it's ready, it shows a **prompt symbol**, usually `$`. It means "ready, type here". You **don't type the `$` yourself**: it's already there.

Type a command after it and press **Enter**. The answer (called **output**) appears on the lines below. Commands are **case-sensitive**: `pwd` works, `PWD` does not.

theory.title: Four commands to find your way
theory.body:
Your computer is a tree of **folders**. The terminal is always standing *inside* one of them.

`pwd` answers "where am I?" (it prints the current folder). `ls` answers "what's here?" (it lists files and folders). `cd folder` means "go into that folder". `cd ..` means "go up one level", back to the parent folder.

A **project** is nothing magic: it's just a folder full of files. In the example, anything after `#` is a note for humans; the terminal ignores it.
theory.code:
$ pwd          # where am I?
/Users/kip
$ ls           # what's here?
projects  notes.md
$ cd projects  # go into projects
$ cd ..        # go back up

theory.title: Inside Claude Code the prompt changes
theory.body:
When you start Claude Code (by typing `claude`), you're now *talking to Claude*, and the prompt looks like `>` instead of `$`.

At the `>` prompt you type **plain English** ("explain this project") or **slash commands** that start with `/`, like `/help`.

Rule of thumb: `$` = the shell, which wants commands like `ls`. `>` = Claude, which understands sentences.

exercises.prompt: Your terminal shows `$` with a blinking cursor. What does the `$` mean?
options: You must type a $ before every command
exercises.explanation: The $ is the prompt: the terminal is waiting for you, and it's already printed so you never type it yourself.

exercises.prompt: Match each command to what it does.
exercises.explanation: These four commands let you look around and move between folders, which is all the navigation you need to start.

exercises.prompt: The terminal shows `$`. You want to list what's in this folder. Which one do you type?
exercises.explanation: The $ is already on screen as the prompt, so you type only the command itself: ls.

exercises.prompt: You started Claude Code and now see a `>` prompt. What can you type there?
options: Only shell commands like ls and pwd
Plain English, or slash commands like /help
exercises.explanation: The > prompt means you're talking to Claude, which understands sentences and slash commands instead of shell commands.

exercises.prompt: Complete Kip's tour: check where you are, list what's here, then go up one folder.
exercises.hint: pwd = where am I, ls = what's here, and two dots (..) mean the folder above.
exercises.explanation: pwd shows your location, ls lists what's inside, and cd .. moves you up to the parent folder.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps of running a command in order.
steps: Type the command, for example pwd
Read the output on the lines below
exercises.explanation: Every command follows the same rhythm: prompt, type, Enter, read the output.

exercises.prompt: Show which folder you're in.
exercises.hint: It's three letters: p-w-d (no $ needed, it's already there).
exercises.explanation: pwd prints the folder the terminal is currently standing in.

exercises.prompt: You're in a folder named projects. Go up one folder.
exercises.hint: cd, a space, then two dots: cd ..
exercises.explanation: cd .. moves you to the parent folder, one level up.

lessons.title: Anatomy of a command
lessons.description: Command names, arguments, flags, quotes and paths, read left to right.

theory.title: Read a command left to right
theory.body:
A command is like a short sentence. Read it **left to right**:

**1. Command name** first: which program to run, like `claude`.

**2. Arguments**: what to work on, like a folder name in `cd projects`.

**3. Flags**: options that change *how* it behaves. Flags start with **dashes**.

Spaces separate the parts, so `claude --continue` is two parts: the program `claude` and the flag `--continue` (continue your last conversation).

theory.title: Flags: long, short, and with values
theory.body:
Flags come in two forms that usually mean the same thing:

**Long form**: two dashes and a word, like `--continue`. Easy to read.

**Short form**: one dash and one letter, like `-c`. Quick to type.

Some flags need a **value** right after them: in `--output-format json`, the flag is `--output-format` and its value is `json`.

If an argument has **spaces**, wrap it in **double quotes** so it stays one piece: `claude "explain this project"` gives Claude the whole sentence as one task.
theory.code:
claude --continue     # long form
claude -c             # short form, same thing
claude --output-format json
claude "explain this project"

theory.title: Paths and file types
theory.body:
A **path** is an address for a file. Slashes separate folders: `src/app.ts` means the file `app.ts` inside the folder `src`.

Shortcuts: `~` means **your home folder**, `.` means **the current folder**, and `..` (you met it already) means the folder above.

The ending of a file name is its **extension** and hints what's inside: `.md` = Markdown notes, `.json` = settings data, `.ts` / `.js` = code, `.sh` = a shell script (a list of commands).
theory.code:
src/app.ts           # app.ts inside the src folder
~/projects           # projects in your home folder
./CLAUDE.md          # CLAUDE.md in the current folder
.claude/settings.json

exercises.prompt: In `claude --continue`, which part is the flag?
exercises.explanation: Flags start with dashes, so --continue is the flag and claude is the command name.

exercises.prompt: Match each piece to what it means.
exercises.explanation: Dashes mark flags, slashes separate folders in a path, and ~ and . are shortcuts for common folders.

exercises.prompt: Which file most likely holds Markdown notes?
exercises.explanation: The .md extension means Markdown, a simple format for notes and documentation.

exercises.prompt: You want to start Claude with the task: explain this project. Which command keeps the task in one piece?
exercises.explanation: Double quotes keep text with spaces together as one argument, so Claude gets the whole sentence as its task.

exercises.prompt: Write the same flag twice: first the long form, then the short form.
exercises.code:
claude ___     # long form
claude ___     # short form
exercises.hint: Long flags use two dashes and a word; short flags use one dash and one letter.
exercises.explanation: --continue and -c are the long and short spellings of the same flag.

exercises.prompt: Read `claude --output-format json` left to right. Put the parts in order.
steps: --output-format: a flag that changes how it behaves
json: the value given to that flag
exercises.explanation: Command name first, then the flag, then the flag's value right after it.

exercises.prompt: Start Claude and continue your last conversation, using the long flag.
exercises.hint: The program name, a space, then two dashes and the word continue.
exercises.explanation: claude --continue opens Claude and picks up your most recent conversation.

exercises.prompt: Start Claude with the task explain this project (remember the quotes).
exercises.hint: claude, a space, then the sentence inside double quotes: claude "..."
exercises.explanation: The quotes turn the whole sentence into one argument, which Claude receives as its first task.

lessons.title: Reading config files
lessons.description: Just enough Markdown and JSON to read CLAUDE.md and settings.json.

theory.title: Markdown: notes with a little structure
theory.body:
Claude Code reads a notes file called `CLAUDE.md`. The `.md` means it's **Markdown**: plain text with a few symbols for structure.

A line starting with `#` and a space is a **heading** (a title). A line starting with `-` and a space is a **bullet** in a list.

That's it. Everything else is normal sentences, written for Claude to read.
theory.code:
# Project notes

- Run tests before committing
- Use 2-space indentation

theory.title: JSON: labeled boxes of settings
theory.body:
Settings live in `.claude/settings.json`, written in **JSON**. The rules are strict, but there are only a few:

Curly braces `{ }` hold **key/value pairs**. The **key** is the label, always in **double quotes**. A **colon** `:` sits between key and value. **Commas** go *between* pairs, but **never after the last one** (no trailing comma).

Text values (called **strings**) are in double quotes too, like `"dark"`. Square brackets `[ ]` hold a **list**, with commas between items.

theory.title: You read, steer and check
theory.body:
A value can itself be another `{ }` box. Just read it from the outside in: here `permissions` holds `allow`, which holds a list.

Good news: you're **not expected to write code from scratch**. In Claude Code, **Claude writes the code**. Your job is to **ask** in plain English, **read** what it changed, **steer** it if something's off, and **check** that it works.

Knowing what `{ }`, `[ ]` and `#` mean is enough to follow along. Kip believes in you.

exercises.prompt: In a Markdown file, what is the line `# Project notes`?
exercises.explanation: In Markdown, # followed by a space turns the line into a heading.

exercises.prompt: Match each symbol to its job.
exercises.explanation: Each symbol has one small job, and recognizing them is most of what reading JSON and Markdown takes.

exercises.prompt: Which settings snippet is valid JSON?
exercises.explanation: JSON forbids a comma after the last pair, so the trailing comma makes the first one invalid.

exercises.prompt: Which of these is a correct JSON key/value pair?
exercises.explanation: JSON keys and text values use double quotes, with a colon in between.

exercises.prompt: Complete this settings file.
exercises.hint: Curly brace opens the box, a colon goes between key and value, a comma between pairs, and a square bracket opens a list.
exercises.explanation: { opens the settings, : links each key to its value, , separates pairs, and [ starts the list that ] closes.

exercises.prompt: Complete this CLAUDE.md: a heading, then a bullet.
exercises.hint: In Markdown, # starts a heading and - starts a bullet.
exercises.explanation: # makes the first line a heading and - makes the second line a list item.

exercises.prompt: Put your role in a Claude Code session in order.
exercises.explanation: You stay in charge by asking, reading, steering and checking, while Claude does the typing.

exercises.prompt: Settings live in the .claude folder. Move into the folder named .claude.
exercises.hint: cd, a space, then the folder name (it starts with a dot): cd .claude
exercises.explanation: cd followed by a folder name moves you into it, here the .claude folder that holds settings.json.

mission.title: Open your terminal for real
mission.intro: Time to leave the practice tank. Open a real terminal on your computer and take Kip's four-command tour. Nothing you do here can break anything.
checklist: Open your terminal app (macOS: Terminal; Windows: PowerShell or Windows Terminal; Linux: your terminal)
Find the prompt symbol waiting for you (often $ or >)
Run pwd to see which folder you're in
Run ls to see what's in it
cd into one of the folders you saw
mission.explanation: You just navigated your computer by typing, which is the exact skill every later unit builds on.

cheatsheet.description: Shell prompt: ready for a command. Don't type it yourself.
Claude Code prompt: type plain English or /commands.
Go into a folder / go up one level.
Flags change how a command behaves; long form has two dashes, short form one.
Keeps text with spaces together as one argument.
Home folder, current folder, parent folder.
Markdown notes for Claude: # heading, - bullet.
JSON settings: { } pairs, "double-quoted" keys, [ ] lists, no trailing comma.
